species.Agelaius phoeniceus: Males flash scarlet-and-yellow shoulder patches from cattail tops as they sing; females are streaky brown and easily mistaken for sparrows. Among the most abundant birds in North American marshes.
species.Aix sponsa: The drake's iridescent green crest and bold white bridle make it one of the most ornate ducks anywhere. Nests in tree cavities; ducklings leap from the hole to the water the day after hatching.
species.Alligator mississippiensis: A broad, rounded snout and a dark, armoured back distinguish it from crocodiles. A keystone of the wetlands: its 'gator holes' hold water through the dry season for fish, wading birds and turtles.
species.Alopochen aegyptiaca: An African shelduck with chocolate eye patches and a pale body, now established across South Florida. Pairs are loud and fiercely territorial around nesting sites.
species.Anas bahamensis: A Caribbean dabbler with bright white cheeks and a red-based bill. Wild birds rarely reach Florida, so most local sightings are escapes from collections.
species.Anas fulvigula: A dark, uniformly brown dabbler with a plain buff face and yellow bill, resident year-round in Florida's freshwater and brackish marshes. Closely related to the Mallard, with which it often hybridises.
species.Anhinga anhinga: Swims with only its snake-like neck above water, then spears fish with its dagger bill. Its feathers lack waterproofing, so it perches with wings spread wide to dry in the sun.
species.Apis mellifera: The familiar honey bee, introduced from Europe and kept worldwide. Foragers communicate the direction and distance of flowers to the hive with a 'waggle dance'.
species.Aramus guarauna: A brown, white-spotted wader whose long, slightly curved bill is shaped for extracting apple snails from their shells. Its wailing scream at night has spooked many a visitor to Florida's swamps.
species.Ardea alba: Tall, all-white and black-legged, with a yellow bill that turns brighter in breeding season, when long lacy plumes grow from the back. Hunts with slow, deliberate patience in open shallows.
species.Ardea cinerea: The Eurasian counterpart of the Great Blue Heron, paler grey and slightly smaller. Very rare in the Americas, so a Florida photo is far more likely a Great Blue Heron.
species.Ardea herodias: North America's largest heron, standing over a metre tall, with blue-grey plumage and a black crown stripe. Florida also hosts its all-white 'Great White Heron' form in the Keys.
species.Ardea pacifica: An Australian heron with a white head and neck set against slate-dark wings. Outside Australia it is seen only in zoos.
species.Arenaria interpres: A stocky shorebird that, true to its name, flips stones, shells and seaweed to find prey. Its harlequin breeding plumage fades to mottled brown in winter.
species.Aythya collaris: A diving duck named for a faint chestnut collar that is almost never visible; the white ring on the bill is the easier field mark. Winters on Florida lakes in large rafts.
species.Baeolophus bicolor: A small grey songbird with a crest, big dark eyes and a rusty wash on the flanks. A bold regular at feeders, often travelling with chickadees and woodpeckers.
species.Balearica regulorum: An East African crane crowned with a spray of golden bristle-like feathers. Its national-bird status in Uganda contrasts with sharp declines in the wild.
species.Bos taurus: Domestic cattle. In Florida pastures they share the field with Cattle Egrets, which feed on insects the herd stirs up.
species.Brachymesia gravida: A large dragonfly whose wings bear four dark spots, one near the tip of each. Common around brackish ponds along Florida's coasts.
species.Bubulcus ibis: A small, stocky white heron that follows cattle and tractors to catch the insects they flush. It colonised the Americas on its own from Africa in the 1870s.
species.Buteo jamaicensis: Its brick-red tail gives it away in flight. The most widespread hawk in North America, often seen perched on roadside poles watching for rodents.
species.Buteo lineatus: Rufous-barred underparts and black-and-white checkered wings mark this woodland hawk. Florida birds are paler and especially vocal, with a ringing 'kee-ah' call.
species.Butorides virescens: A small, stocky heron with a chestnut neck and glossy green-black back. One of the few tool-using birds, it sometimes drops bait on the water to lure fish.
species.Cairina moschata: Wild birds are glossy black with white wing patches; feral Florida birds show red facial skin and every mix of colours. Native to Central and South America.
species.Calidris alba: The classic little sandpiper that chases retreating waves on sandy beaches like a wind-up toy. Pale grey in winter, it breeds in the High Arctic.
species.Callinectes sapidus: Its scientific name means 'savoury beautiful swimmer'. Paddle-shaped rear legs make it a strong swimmer, and adult males have bright blue claws.
species.Canis lupus: Domestic dog. Kept here as a record of the day rather than a wildlife sighting.
species.Cardinalis cardinalis: The brilliant red male with a black mask is unmistakable; the female is warm buff with red highlights. Both sing, often from a high exposed perch.
species.Casuarius casuarius: A massive flightless bird of Australian and New Guinean rainforests, with a casque on its head and dagger-like inner toes. Seen in Florida only in zoos.
species.Cathartes aura: Soars on wings held in a shallow V, rocking unsteadily as it searches. Unusually for a bird, it finds carrion largely by smell.
species.Celithemis elisa: A small dragonfly with amber-patched wings and a calico pattern of brown spots. Prefers ponds with plenty of emergent vegetation.
species.Celithemis eponina: Orange-washed wings banded with brown make this one of the most striking dragonflies in the Southeast. Often perches at the very tip of a stem.
species.Crocothemis servilia: A brilliant red Asian skimmer, introduced to South Florida and spreading. Males perch on stems over still water.
species.Dacelo novaeguineae: Australia's famous 'laughing' kingfisher, a large, stocky bird that hunts lizards, snakes and insects. Seen outside Australia only in zoos.
species.Dendrocygna autumnalis: A long-legged duck with a coral-pink bill and black belly that perches readily in trees. Named for its whistled calls, it has spread rapidly through Florida.
species.Dryobates pubescens: North America's smallest woodpecker, with a short bill and a red nape patch on males. It forages even on the thin stems of weeds and goldenrod.
species.Dryocopus pileatus: A crow-sized woodpecker with a flaming red crest that carves rectangular holes in dead trees. Its loud, laughing call carries far through Florida's hammocks.
species.Dumetella carolinensis: A slate-grey songbird with a black cap and a rusty patch under the tail. Its mewing call explains the name; its song strings together borrowed phrases.
species.Egretta caerulea: Adults are slate-blue with purplish heads; first-year birds are pure white with blue-grey bill bases. White young often feed alongside Snowy Egrets, which lets them catch more fish.
species.Egretta garzetta: The Old World twin of the Snowy Egret, separated by subtle differences in lores and plumes. Very rare in Florida, so a white egret with yellow feet is far more likely a Snowy.
species.Egretta novaehollandiae: A grey Australasian heron with a white face. Outside its range it is seen only in zoos.
species.Egretta rufescens: Famous for its 'drunken' hunting dance, lurching and wing-flicking to herd fish in shallow flats. Comes in a dark morph with a shaggy rufous head and a rarer all-white morph.
species.Egretta thula: A dainty white egret with a black bill and bright yellow 'golden slippers' on black legs. Its nuptial plumes were once worth more than gold to milliners.
species.Egretta tricolor: A slender, long-necked heron with a white belly that contrasts with blue-grey upperparts. Often hunts actively, running and wing-flicking through the shallows.
species.Elanoides forficatus: Perhaps the most graceful raptor in North America, with a deeply forked tail and crisp black-and-white plumage. It eats on the wing, snatching insects and small reptiles from treetops.
species.Eudocimus albus: All white with a decurved coral-red bill and black wing tips that show in flight. Probes mud by touch, and flocks move to roost in long lines at dusk.
species.Falco sparverius: North America's smallest falcon, colourful and often seen hovering over fields. It perches on wires, pumping its tail.
species.Fulica americana: A dark, duck-like rail with a white bill, gathering in large winter flocks on open water. Lobed toes rather than webbed feet power its swimming.
species.Gallinula galeata: A dark marsh bird with a red frontal shield and yellow-tipped bill, walking on lily pads on long toes. Chicks are black balls of down with bald red heads.
species.Geothlypis trichas: A small warbler; the male wears a black bandit mask over a bright yellow throat. It sings a rolling 'witchety-witchety' from dense marsh vegetation.
species.Gyps africanus: A critically endangered African vulture, with populations collapsing from poisoning. Seen in Florida only in zoos.
species.Gyps coprotheres: Southern Africa's large cliff-nesting vulture, now endangered. Seen in Florida only in zoos.
species.Iguana iguana: An introduced Central and South American lizard, now widespread in South Florida, where it basks in trees over canals. Males turn orange in breeding season.
species.Lanius ludovicianus: A grey songbird with a black mask that hunts like a tiny raptor, impaling prey on thorns or barbed wire. Declining across much of North America.
species.Leucophaeus atricilla: A coastal gull with a dark hood in summer and a laughing call that gives it its name. Common on Florida beaches year-round.
species.Lontra canadensis: Sleek and playful, this otter travels between wetlands and is often seen fishing in pairs or family groups. Florida birders know it from canals and spring runs.
species.Lontra longicaudis: A Central and South American otter. In Florida a wild otter is almost certainly the North American River Otter.
species.Lophodytes cucullatus: The drake raises a fan-shaped white crest edged in black; the female's crest is a shaggy cinnamon. A winter diver that chases small fish underwater.
species.Lophura erythrophthalma: A Southeast Asian pheasant of lowland forest, now near threatened. Seen in Florida only in zoos and bird parks.
species.Macaca mulatta: An Asian monkey whose Florida population descends from animals released along the Silver River in the 1930s. The colony is now the subject of active management.
species.Megaceryle alcyon: Stocky with a shaggy blue-grey crest; unusually, the female wears the extra rusty belly band. Rattles loudly as it flies along the water.
species.Melanerpes carolinus: Named for a faint reddish wash on the belly rather than the obvious red cap and nape. A common, noisy woodpecker of Florida yards and hammocks.
species.Melanerpes erythrocephalus: The only eastern woodpecker with an entirely crimson head, set off by bold white wing patches. It caches acorns and insects in crevices.
species.Mimus gilvus: The Caribbean and Central American relative of the Northern Mockingbird. Very rare in Florida, so most mockingbirds here are Northern.
species.Mimus polyglottos: Florida's state bird, a tireless mimic that may know more than 200 songs and sings through the night in spring. Flashes white wing patches when it displays.
species.Mycteria americana: North America's only breeding stork, with a bald grey head and a heavy bill that snaps shut on fish by touch. Breeding success tracks Everglades water levels.
species.Myiarchus crinitus: A loud, lemon-bellied flycatcher of the treetops with a whistled 'wheep!'. It famously lines its nest cavity with shed snakeskin.
species.Nannopterum auritum: Named for two small breeding tufts rarely noticed in the field; the orange throat skin is the reliable field mark. Swims low in the water and dives for fish.
species.Nyctanassa violacea: A stocky night heron with a black-and-white striped face and buff crown. It specialises in crabs and crayfish.
species.Nycticorax nycticorax: A compact heron with a black cap and back and red eyes, active at dusk and through the night. Young birds are streaky brown with yellow-green legs.
species.Oxyura jamaicensis: A compact diving duck with a stiff tail often held cocked. Breeding males turn rusty with a sky-blue bill.
species.Pandion haliaetus: The fish hawk: dives feet-first and carries its catch head-forward for less drag. Ospreys returned across Florida after the DDT ban.
species.Passerina cyanea: The male is entirely blue, a colour made by feather structure rather than pigment. Migrates at night, navigating partly by the stars.
species.Pelecanus occidentalis: Plunge-dives from height, folding its wings just before impact. Its recovery from pesticide-era declines is one of conservation's success stories.
species.Phyciodes tharos: A small orange-and-black butterfly that is one of the commonest in open fields. Named for the pale crescent on the underside of the hindwing.
species.Platalea ajaja: Pink plumage, from carotenoids in its crustacean diet, and a spatulate bill swept side to side through the water. In the U.S. it breeds mainly in Florida and along the Texas coast.
species.Podilymbus podiceps: A small, chunky diver with a thick bill ringed in black in breeding season. It sinks slowly out of sight rather than diving when alarmed.
species.Polioptila caerulea: A tiny, slim blue-grey bird with a long white-edged tail that it flicks constantly. Its nest is bound with spider silk and camouflaged with lichen.
species.Porphyrio martinica: Iridescent purple and green with a sky-blue shield and red-and-yellow bill, it walks on lily pads on enormously long toes. Among the most photogenic birds of Florida's marshes.
species.Primolius maracana: A small South American macaw with green plumage and blue flight feathers. Seen in Florida only in collections and parks.
species.Procyon lotor: The masked raccoon, a clever generalist of wetlands, woods and towns. Its sensitive front paws 'see' food by touch underwater.
species.Pseudemys peninsularis: A large basking turtle of Florida springs and rivers, often stacked on logs. Marked with 'hairpin' stripes on the head.
species.Quiscalus major: Large and long-tailed; males are glossy blue-black with yellow eyes, females warm brown. Noisy and bold around coastal marshes and parking lots.
species.Quiscalus quiscula: Smaller and shorter-tailed than the Boat-tailed Grackle, with an iridescent bronze or purple sheen. Often in large flocks on lawns.
species.Rostrhamus sociabilis: An apple-snail specialist with a fine hooked bill for extracting snails. In the U.S. it breeds only in Florida, where it is endangered.
species.Sayornis phoebe: A modest grey-brown flycatcher that wags its tail constantly and says its name. One of the first migrants to return in spring.
species.Sciurus carolinensis: The familiar grey squirrel, a key planter of oaks through forgotten acorn caches.
species.Setophaga americana: A small warbler with a blue back, yellow throat and a greenish 'saddle'. Breeds where Spanish moss hangs, which it uses for its nest.
species.Setophaga palmarum: A brownish warbler that bobs its tail constantly while feeding on the ground. One of the commonest wintering warblers in Florida.
species.Setophaga ruticilla: Males are black with flaming orange patches; females wear yellow. It fans its tail to flush insects.
species.Spinus tristis: In winter, the male trades its bright yellow plumage for a dull olive coat. Feeds almost entirely on seeds.
species.Strix varia: A large brown-eyed owl whose call is rendered 'who cooks for you, who cooks for you-all'. Often hunts in daylight in Florida swamps.
species.Sturnus vulgaris: Introduced to New York in 1890, it now numbers in the tens of millions across North America. Winter plumage is spangled with white spots.
species.Sylvilagus palustris: A dark, short-eared rabbit of Florida's wetlands that swims readily. Unlike most rabbits, it often walks rather than hops.
species.Threskiornis molucca: Australia's 'bin chicken', an urban scavenger with a bare black head. Seen outside Australia only in zoos.
species.Tramea carolina: A large dragonfly with dark red 'saddlebag' patches at the base of its hindwings. Often glides high over ponds.
species.Tringa solitaria: Usually alone, as its name says, on the muddy edges of freshwater ponds. A dark-backed sandpiper with white eye-rings.
species.Varanus komodoensis: The largest living lizard, native to a handful of Indonesian islands. Seen in Florida only in zoos.
species.Varecia variegata: A critically endangered Madagascan lemur with a loud chorus call. Seen in Florida only in zoos.
